primary_text_note: Novel in copyright. Quotations verified against a full-text concordance (lak12.com/quote-classic/lordofflies), GradeSaver, CliffsNotes, Shmoop, eNotes, americanliterature.com and the Nobel Prize biography.

findings.claim: “For Eduqas Component 2, Section A, context is assessed through AO4 (up to 5 marks in the (b) response).”
findings.truth: AO4 is accurate written English (spelling, punctuation, sentence range), not context. The post-1914 prose section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only — there is no AO3, so context earns nothing on this question. It is one source-based question worth 40 marks with no (a)/(b) parts, and the board is never named in student text.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md sec 2.2 + 3.1: “Section A (20%) Post 1914 Prose/Drama (40 marks)… through a source based response… Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4”; AO4 defined as “Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures… with accurate spelling and punctuation”.

findings.claim: “Golding’s WWII experience — including D-Day and witnessing the Holocaust — convinced him…”
findings.truth: Golding served in the Royal Navy 1940–45 (the Bismarck action, D-Day, Walcheren). He did not witness the camps; he reacted to the post-war news of them.
findings.evidence: nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1983/golding/biographical/ ; cliffsnotes.com/literature/l/lord-of-the-flies/about-lord-of-the-flies-2 (“the world was horrified by news of the Nazi death camps”).

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: “Witnessing the liberation of concentration camps.”
findings.truth: Same fabrication as F2. Replaced with his actual war service.

findings.claim: “Ralph references The Coral Island directly in Chapter 2: ‘It’s like in a book… Treasure Island… Coral Island’.”
findings.truth: Ralph says only “It’s like in a book.” The titles (Treasure Island — Swallows and Amazons — Coral Island) are then babbled by the other boys.

findings.claim: All six questions tagged “[20]” and “20 marks — Extract Analysis / Wider Text Response”, with band ladder 17-20 down to 1-4; Q2 mark scheme says “AO4 context embedded throughout.”
findings.truth: The prose section is a single 40-mark source-based question. A 20+20 extract/essay split is another board’s format. Marks, labels and band ranges corrected to 40 (33-40 / 25-32 / 17-24 / 9-16 / 1-8); the AO4-as-context line removed.

findings.claim: “[Jack] is visibly furious at losing. His face goes ‘ugly without silliness’.”
findings.truth: “ugly without silliness” belongs to Jack’s first physical description in Ch. 1 (“His face was crumpled and freckled, and ugly without silliness”), not to the election result. The vote line is “the freckles on Jack’s face disappeared under a blush of mortification”.

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which phrase describes Ralph’s appearance?” → “‘Ugly without silliness.’”
findings.truth: The phrase describes Jack, not Ralph. The lesson’s own prose says Jack. A student learning this card would misattribute a key quotation.

findings.claim: “Piggy discovers a conch shell” / “The conch is found by Piggy but blown by Ralph” / KC “Who finds the conch shell on the beach?” keyed to Piggy / L6 “He finds the conch” / L7 “Found by Piggy and blown by Ralph” / L7 flashcard “Piggy spots it in the lagoon”.
findings.truth: In Ch. 1 RALPH spots the creamy shell in the lagoon; Piggy recognises it as a conch and tells Ralph how to blow it. The knowledge check marked the true answer (Ralph) wrong. Reworded so Piggy still owns the knowledge — the thematic point survives — but the plot fact is right.
findings.evidence: americanliterature.com Ch. 1 summary + enotes “Who discovered the conch in Lord of the Flies?”: “Ralph spots something cream-coloured in the lagoon… Piggy correctly identifies the object as a conch shell”.

findings.claim: The choir arrives in ‘black cloaks’ with ‘silver crosses’.
findings.truth: The text reads “black cloaks which bore a long silver cross on the left breast” — one cross per cloak, singular.

findings.claim: “For the Eduqas (a) extract question…”
findings.truth: There is no part (a). One 40-mark source-based question; board not named in student text.

findings.claim: 20-mark labels and band ladder, as F5; Q4/Q6 mark schemes say Piggy “finds” the conch.
findings.truth: As F5 and F8.

findings.claim: “Even Ralph is momentarily seduced: ‘What a place for a fort!’”
findings.truth: Jack says “What a place for a fort!” in Ch. 6. The lesson’s own flashcard already credits Jack, so the two contradicted each other.
findings.evidence: curvelearn.com/2013/08/lord-of-flies-quotes-chapter-six-beast.html (“Jack was excited. ‘What a place for a fort!’”); bookrags.com/notes/lof/part6.html

findings.claim: “Ralph is ‘savage with unformulated knowledge’.”
findings.truth: No such wording in the novel; “unformulated” does not occur. The invented quotation is removed rather than replaced, since no real wording could be located for that moment.
findings.evidence: lak12.com/quote-classic/lordofflies?s=unformulated — no result; the six indexed “knowledge” sentences do not include it; web search for the exact phrase returns nothing.

findings.claim: “Ralph asks: ‘What are we? Humans? Or animals? Or savages?’”
findings.truth: Piggy speaks this line in the Ch. 5 assembly.

findings.claim: “In the (a) response… In the (b) response… for Eduqas”
findings.truth: As F10.

findings.claim: 20-mark labels and band ladder.
findings.truth: As F5.

findings.claim: “He realises the sea is ‘a barrier, a prison’.”
findings.truth: The Ch. 7 text is “This was the divider, the barrier.” The word “prison” does not occur in the novel.

findings.claim: “For the Eduqas (a) extract question on Chapters 7–9…”
findings.truth: As F10.

findings.claim: 20-mark labels and band ladder.
findings.truth: As F5.

findings.claim: “For the Eduqas (b) whole-text response…”
findings.truth: As F10.

findings.claim: 20-mark labels and band ladder.
findings.truth: As F5.

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which JACK line opposes democracy to violence?” → “Which is better — to have rules and agree, or to hunt and kill?”
findings.truth: That is Piggy’s final speech at Castle Rock (Ch. 11). The lesson’s own prose says “When Piggy asks…”. The same card is wrong again in L8.
findings.evidence: Ch. 11 text, widely quoted; the lesson’s own content_html contradicts the card.

findings.claim: “He is often confused, unable to articulate what he feels: ‘Ralph was a specialist in thought now, and could recognise thought in another.’”
findings.truth: The quotation says the opposite of the claim — in Ch. 5 it follows Ralph recognising that Piggy has brains, and marks Ralph becoming a thinker. Replaced with Ralph’s own line “I can’t think. Not like Piggy.”, which does support the point.

findings.claim: “For Eduqas character questions…”
findings.truth: House rule: the board is never named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: house style rule for Eduqas/WJEC lessons.

findings.claim: 20-mark labels and band ladder; Q4 mark scheme repeats “Finds conch”.
findings.truth: As F5 and F8.

findings.claim: “For Eduqas, symbols are a powerful tool for the (b) whole-text response… with embedded context linking to Golding’s post-war pessimism.”
findings.truth: No part (b); and context is not an assessment objective on this question, so telling students to embed it for marks is mark-affecting.

findings.claim: 20-mark labels and band ladder; Q2 mark scheme ends “AO4 context.”
findings.truth: As F5 — AO4 is accurate written English, and context is not credited here.

findings.claim: “Post-1914 prose papers typically pair a printed extract with a wider-text task on the whole novel… Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark split and time allocation.”
findings.truth: The paper is 2 hours 30 minutes and carries three 40-mark sections. The post-1914 prose task is ONE source-based question worth 40 marks with an extract printed, closed book. There is no separate extract task and wider-text task and no unknown mark split.

findings.claim: Key fact: “Wider-text tasks add context (AO4), which must be woven into analysis…” (plus a revision prompt asking which task “weaves in context”).
findings.truth: AO4 is accurate written English. The section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only; there is no AO3 and context earns no marks here.

findings.claim: “For Eduqas: part (a) = close analysis of the extract (AO1 + AO2); part (b) = wider exploration with context (AO1 + AO2 + AO4).”
findings.truth: As F28 and F29.

findings.claim: The whole tip teaches how to keep part (a) and part (b) separate.
findings.truth: As F28 — the format described does not exist on this paper. Rewritten around the single source-based answer, including that accurate writing carries marks.

findings.claim: KC2 “In the Eduqas exam, which part of the question assesses context (AO4)?” keyed to “Part (b) only”; KC3 “Part (a) focuses on the ___ while part (b) asks about elsewhere in the text.”
findings.truth: Both items test an invented two-part format and a false definition of AO4. Rewritten: KC2 now asks which objectives the question credits (AO1, AO2 and AO4); KC3 asks what is printed on the paper. Both keys stay at index 1.

findings.claim: Cards: “Which JACK quote frames the democratic/savage binary?”; “Which AO is only assessed in Part (b)…?” → “AO4 — context.”; “Which AOs are assessed in Part (a)?”; “Mixing extract analysis into Part (b)…”
findings.truth: The first misattributes Piggy’s line (see F22); the other three rehearse a format that does not exist and define AO4 as context.

findings.claim: “AO4: Assessment Objective 4: understanding of context (only assessed in part (b) for Eduqas).”
findings.truth: AO4 is accurate written English — vocabulary, sentence structures, spelling and punctuation.

findings.claim: Description names the board (“Eduqas exam strategy”); six questions tagged 20 marks; three ask about the theme “elsewhere in the text”.
findings.truth: Board removed; marks and band ranges corrected to 40; “elsewhere in the text” (which presumes a part (a)) changed to “across the novel”.

findings.claim: Even after relabelling, the bank still models two kinds of task — “extract” questions and “whole novel” questions — each now worth the full 40 marks.
findings.truth: Two defensible options. (a) Keep as done: every question is a full 40-mark source-based task, matching what the sibling Eduqas post-1914 units (never-let-me-go, the-woman-in-black, a-taste-of-honey) already ship; students practise both halves of the skill separately. (b) Rewrite each stem to ask for the extract AND the rest of the novel in one question, which mirrors the real paper more closely but touches all 48 question stems. Recommendation: (a) — consistent with the units already fixed, and L8 now teaches explicitly that one answer must do both jobs.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md sec 2.2 + 3.1; sibling unit _edits.json files under scripts/_retrofc/units/english-literature-eduqas__*.

findings.claim: “Jack responds… by punching Piggy” (also L7 content and flashcard).
findings.truth: The text has Jack “smacked Piggy’s head”, knocking the glasses off so one lens breaks. Not mark-affecting.

findings.claim: “R.M. Ballantyne’s The Coral Island (1858)”
findings.truth: It went on sale in late 1857 with an 1858 title page. Both dates are defensible and 1858 is widely printed.

findings.claim: The pig’s head “grinning ‘cynically’”.
findings.truth: The novel attaches cynicism to the head’s “half-shut eyes… dim with the infinite cynicism of adult life” (Ch. 8) and has the skull “jeer at him cynically” (Ch. 12). The single word is in the novel and attached to the same object, so no edit.

findings.claim: “Which excuse do Piggy and Ralph offer…” → “‘We was scared!’”
findings.truth: Piggy speaks the line, but he speaks for both of them (“we”), so the card is loose rather than wrong.

findings.claim: Nine “Define ‘X’…” flashcard questions end in a full stop, and L8 content carries only 2 dfn glossary terms against a house floor of 3.
findings.truth: Pre-existing validator nits, not fact errors. Left alone — out of scope for the fact-check.

summary: Every lesson carried the same mark-affecting exam error: the unit teaches a two-part (a)/(b) paper worth 20+20 with AO4 as context, when the spec sets ONE 40-mark source-based question assessing AO1, AO2 and AO4 with no AO3 and no context credit. L8 is built almost entirely on that invented format. On top of that: four quotation/speaker errors (‘ugly without silliness’ given to Ralph and to the wrong moment, ‘What a place for a fort!’ given to Ralph, ‘What are we? Humans?…’ given to Ralph, Piggy’s ‘Which is better…’ given to Jack twice), two fabricated quotations (‘a barrier, a prison’, ‘savage with unformulated knowledge’), a false biography claim (Golding witnessing the Holocaust) repeated in a flashcard, and a plot error repeated across three lessons and a knowledge check (Piggy “finds” the conch; Ralph spots it). 196 edits; 0 lessons clean.
